# 4. Restorative Functions {#sec-functions}

Two solar farms in the same county, the same size, the same panels, the same crop ground underneath. Under one, gravel and a herbicide schedule; under the other, a planting rooted deep enough to hold a summer storm where it falls.

Nothing about the land separates them. Where a project sits (§1) and what happened to the farming on it (§2) set the outer limits of what is possible there, but what the ground actually ends up doing is settled by how the design resolved its competing pressures (§3), and above all by whether anyone was still pushing for restoration when the cheaper option was on the table.

*Restorative* is therefore not something a piece of ground is. It is something a design produces, and on most sites it can be produced or withheld. **Restorative functions** name the five things a design can be aimed at.

- **Water** (§4.1) — what soaks in, what runs off, and what the aquifer gets back
- **Soil and carbon** (§4.2) — what builds back up underneath
- **Habitat** (§4.3) — what can live there
- **Microclimate** (§4.4) — shade, temperature, and moisture right at the ground
- **Community and economy** (§4.5) — what the people hosting it actually get

**A function is not a position on the sharing–sparing axis.** A project holds exactly one position, which records what happened to agricultural production on its ground (§2). It can deliver several functions at once, and the same function turns up at many different positions: pollinator habitat is reachable under grazing (S2), on ordinary converted ground (S3), and on spared or retired ground (S4–S5) alike. That is why habitat is a function and not a sixth position. The three registers stay distinct: a pressure is a force pushing on the design, a lever is an instrument the design uses, and a function is the result the two produce. Treat the five as a palette rather than a scorecard, since no project is expected to deliver all of them and some work against each other.

**A note on "co-benefits."** The field usually calls these co-benefits. The word is worth handling with care: it is an umbrella term with acknowledged definitional ambivalence, and its grammar quietly demotes what it names, since a *co-*benefit is something that arrives alongside the real objective [@mayrhofer2016]. That is the opposite of what this document argues. The functions below are named as objectives, which is why the lexicon says *restorative function* and keeps *co-benefit* for describing how others frame the same ground.

Each section sets out mechanism, design dependencies, which sites can deliver it, its point of use, and evidence status.

## The five functions {#sec-the-functions}

### 4.1 Hydrologic function {#sec-fn-hydrologic}

**Mechanism.** An array reshapes the site water balance. Panels intercept rainfall and redistribute it, concentrating flow along drip lines at panel edges while sheltering the ground beneath, which alters the partition between infiltration, runoff, and evaporation. Shade lowers soil-surface evaporation and plant transpiration, so soil moisture is generally retained; altered cover and compaction change infiltration capacity; and the net effect on deep percolation, groundwater recharge, and stormwater runoff depends on how the ground layer and grading are designed. Restorative hydrologic design uses the array and its ground layer deliberately: to raise infiltration and recharge, to slow and filter runoff (reducing erosion and nutrient export), and to buffer soil moisture through dry spells. At a larger scale the array can change the water *budget*, not just the on-site balance: where solar displaces irrigated cropland it retires that field's consumptive use and saves groundwater at the basin scale [@stid2022; @stid2025], which is the demand-side logic of [water-sustainability solar](5-archetypes.qmd#arch-water) (§5). That saving holds only where groundwater governance keeps it from being pumped elsewhere [@zwickle2021].

**Design dependencies.** Ground-layer composition is primary, since deep-rooted perennial cover infiltrates where bare or gravel ground sheds. Panel and row geometry set where drip concentrates; grading and the placement logic of [solar prairie strips](5-archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) (siting along hydrologic features) put infiltration where runoff collects; the operational regime and the choice of ground cover carry the rest. The instrument migrates along the transect exactly as the [restoration modes](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) do: siting-led along hydrologic features at A2–A3, management-led through ground cover at A4–A5.

**Which sites can deliver it.** Broadly available, because water moves through every site, but most *legible* where the ground layer is designed for it (S2–S5: grazing, prairie/buffer, restored marginal and retired ground) and least so under bare-ground or gravel management. Solar prairie strips are its characteristic siting-led case; managed perennial cover is its characteristic case at scale.

**Point of use.** The widest spread of any function. Soil moisture is **on-site**; slowed, filtered runoff and reduced sediment and nutrient export are **downstream**, used wherever the water goes rather than on the ground that produced them; and retired consumptive use is **regional**, easing an aquifer across a whole management area. The direction matters as much as the distance: ground upslope of a problem can fix it, and identical ground downslope cannot.

::: {.evidence}
**Evidence status.** The dryland microclimate-to-soil-moisture link is **verified** [@barrongafford2019; @sturchio2025; @pinos2026], though effect size is bounded at some sites [@kannenberg2023]. Evidence for infiltration, recharge, and stormwater effects at depth remains thinner [@yavari2022]. Perennial cover has stronger evidence for nutrient-load reduction than for whole water-balance change: it cuts nutrient runoff in cropped landscapes by as much as 85%, and the avoided nitrogen and phosphorus loads from retiring corn-ethanol ground are quantified in [§2.1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) [@sturchio2025croplands]. Treat recharge claims as a field-measurement question rather than a presumed outcome.
:::

### 4.2 Soil & carbon function {#sec-fn-soil}

**Mechanism.** The array changes what the soil is asked to do. Where perennial, low-disturbance cover replaces a tilled row-crop baseline, roots stay in the ground year-round, traffic and tillage fall away, and soil organic carbon and aggregate stability can build back. That is the standard perennialization pathway, here running under and between the panels. The array's own shade and reduced evaporative demand alter the decomposition and moisture regimes that govern how fast carbon accumulates or turns over. Restorative soil design treats the ground layer as the working surface: perennial establishment, minimal disturbance, and a management regime that keeps cover continuous rather than resetting it. Construction cuts the other way, since grading, trenching, and compaction during installation strip and disturb soil, so the early ledger can show a loss before it shows a gain.

**Design dependencies.** Ground-layer composition and establishment method are primary, since a deep-rooted perennial or native mix under no-till builds where an annual, tilled understory does not. Grazing regime and stocking density set whether animal return of nutrients and trampling help or compact; construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline decide how much of the starting soil is lost to the build. As with the hydrologic function, the instrument is siting-led early on the transect (which ground is disturbed, and how) and management-led at scale (the ground cover and grazing regime carried over years). The gains are slow and cumulative, so the operational regime, sustained rather than one-time, carries most of the outcome.

**Which sites can deliver it.** Most reachable under perennial and grazed cover and native-grassland restoration (S2–S3), where the ground layer is designed for continuity, and on restored marginal or retired ground (S4–S5) recovering from a degraded baseline. Least available under annual tillage inside full-sharing cropping (S1) or wherever disturbance is frequent, since each reset spends the accumulated carbon. Regenerative solar grazing and solar prairie strips are its characteristic cases; the marginal-land-solar case depends on how degraded the starting soil was.

**Point of use.** Almost entirely **on-site**, since soil is the one thing that stays put, which makes this the function most fully captured by whoever holds the ground. Carbon is the exception and the limiting case. Sequestration is **global**, benefiting everywhere and no one in particular, which is why it needs a market or a policy behind it before it is worth anything to the person holding the land.

::: {.evidence}
**Evidence status.** Early soil-carbon and surface gains are **verified** for ecovoltaic grassland restoration [@krasner2025], but construction can produce an initial loss and long-run accumulation remains thinly measured [@carvalho2024]. Baseline land cover sets the sign: perennialization can improve a tilled row-crop baseline, while conversion of existing grassland can create a soil-carbon debt [@merheb2025].
:::

### 4.3 Biodiversity & habitat function {#sec-fn-biodiversity}

*Pollinator habitat* and *native grassland* belong here: both are functions, reachable across S2–S5, rather than positions of their own on the sharing–sparing axis.

**Mechanism.** Habitat is built from the ground layer up. Floral plantings supply nectar and pollen; the vegetation's vertical and horizontal structure supplies nesting substrate, cover, and the heterogeneity that lets many species partition a single site, so pollinators, ground-nesting arthropods, and grassland birds find resources an annual monoculture does not offer. Panel shade also shifts the timing: partial shading delays bloom and increases late-season floral abundance [@graham2021]. The array furniture adds its own structure, and the management regime that keeps the planting diverse and undisturbed does as much as the seed mix. Restorative habitat design uses the interrows and array margins as the working habitat, not incidental green space.

**Design dependencies.** Seed-mix composition sets the ceiling, since a native, floral-rich mix reaches species a turf understory cannot. Mowing and grazing *timing* is decisive, not merely their presence: disturbance during nesting or bloom undoes the resource it was meant to provide, so the operational calendar is a design lever in its own right [@blaydes2022]. Fragmentation geometry and the [influence-zone](7-terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) edge matter, because several small arrays scattered through a landscape connect and edge differently than a few large ones, and edge-to-area ratio shapes which species the site reaches. As with the other functions, the instrument is siting-led where placement stitches into existing corridors and management-led where the ground cover and its calendar carry the habitat over years.

**Which sites can deliver it.** Obtainable from the productive middle right through the removal end (S2–S5), via wildflower interrows over grazing (S2), dedicated habitat plantings on converted ground (S3), and restored or retired parcels (S4–S5), which is exactly why it reads as a function reachable at many positions rather than one. Least available under bare-ground, gravel, or intensively disturbed understories. Solar prairie strips and regenerative solar grazing are its characteristic cases.

**Point of use.** **On-site** as habitat, and **adjacent** as service. This is the best-quantified spillover in agrisolar: about 3,500 km² of US farmland sits within 1.5 km of existing and planned utility-scale facilities, roughly a pollinator's foraging distance, and close enough to gain from plantings on them [@walston2018], and pollinators from solar sites have since been recorded visiting soybean in neighboring fields [@walston2024]. At **regional** range it reads differently again, as connectivity in a habitat network rather than as a service to the farm next door [@walston2025].

::: {.evidence}
**Evidence status.** **Verified** for grassland-bird gains [@walston2025], insect-community response [@walston2024], and bee-species diversity in pollinator-planted arrays [@bruningasocolar2025]; scorecards codify the choices, though what each credits differs [@epri2021]. The gain is **context-dependent**: it is largest where the surrounding landscape is already sparse in semi-natural habitat and smaller where that habitat is abundant. Its size is set by what the site would otherwise have been, not by the planting alone.
:::

### 4.4 Microclimate & thermal–water buffering function {#sec-fn-microclimate}

**Mechanism.** The array rewrites the near-surface energy balance. Panels intercept and redistribute incoming radiation, so daytime soil and canopy temperatures fall in their shade, longwave sheltering raises nighttime minima, and the vapor-pressure deficit under the array drops, so the microenvironment swings less far in both directions across the day. That buffering couples tightly to the [hydrologic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-hydrologic): the same shade that cuts thermal extremes also cuts evaporative demand, so moisture is retained and the two functions rise and fall together. Restorative microclimate design tunes the geometry so the shelter lands where a heat- or water-stressed ground layer needs it, without starving it of the light it still requires.

**Design dependencies.** Module geometry and mounting height, row spacing and ground-coverage ratio, and tracking schedule set how much radiation is redistributed and where the shade falls through the day. For crops, the shade-tolerance match is decisive, because the buffering is a benefit only where the ground layer can trade light for relief and a cost where it cannot. The effect is inseparable from scale and array geometry: the same panels that shelter a dryland understory can over-shade a light-limited one, which is why this function turns on the design tipping-point rather than existing uniformly. The instrument is geometry-led throughout, and its sign flips with climate and crop.

**Which sites can deliver it.** Pronounced in hot, water-limited settings and for shade-tolerant ground layers, where lowered temperature and vapor-pressure deficit relieve real stress; muted to adverse in cool or humid settings and for light-demanding crops, where the shade subtracts more than it buffers. It is itself scale- and geometry-dependent, the [design tipping-point noted in §1.1](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude), so its availability is set by the array's form and the site's climate together, not by position on the sharing–sparing axis alone.

**Point of use.** **On-site**, and nowhere else. The buffering exists only under and immediately around the panels, which is why it can be verified directly and why it never appears in an argument about what a project does for the surrounding area. It is the cleanest case of provider and beneficiary being the same ground.

::: {.evidence}
**Evidence status.** The physics is **verified**, and so is the dryland benefit: agrivoltaic and ecovoltaic microclimates redistribute radiation and buffer temperature and moisture [@sturchio2023; @sturchio2025; @pinos2026; @barrongafford2019], water-use efficiency rises under shaded pasture [@adeh2018], and modeling reproduces the soil-moisture response [@wu2022]. The buffering is not uniform in the way the dryland framing implies: across reported sites the soil-moisture gain rises with annual precipitation rather than falling with it, and module cooling strengthens with ambient temperature, reaching about 10 °C over vegetated ground in hot climates [@merheb2025]. Crop-facing magnitudes stay **climate- and crop-conditional**.
:::

### 4.5 Community & economic function {#sec-fn-community}

The one function that is not about the land, and the [SCALE](#sec-scale) **Communities** domain read as an outcome. The other four ask what the ground can provide. This one asks what the people hosting the project actually get. It is the result that the [social-license pressure](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) and the [community-benefit lever](7-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) are aiming at, not another name for them. Three things sit inside it: **economic prosperity**, meaning durable local income and tax base; **livability**, meaning whether people can live alongside the thing and had a real say in it; and **health & equity**, meaning whether the burdens and the benefits land on the same people.

**Mechanism.** A project returns value to its host in several currencies at once: lease and royalty income to the landowner, PILOT and tax revenue to the jurisdiction, wages to local trades through build and O&M, subscription savings to community-solar members, and, where ownership is structured for it, an equity stake rather than only a rent. Diversified income can be the difference that keeps a marginal farm solvent, which is the organizing logic of [marginal land solar](5-archetypes.qmd#arch-marginal). The livability and equity sub-capacities turn less on the size of the payment than on the *procedure*: engagement early enough to shape the design, and a distribution of benefit and burden the community reads as fair. This is why benefit and acceptance come apart: a check without a fair process reads as a bribe (§3.1).

Two figures give the lease argument its size. Landowners leasing cropland to solar earn three to four times more per acre than most crops return at current market prices [@sturchio2025croplands], and where production continues alongside the array the reported gains from the same ground run higher still, roughly 15 times for a vineyard and 10 to 22 times for rabbit pasture [@merheb2025]. Even where co-location does not improve yields at all, the systems can stay profitable [@merheb2025]. The consequence runs past the balance sheet. Federal biofuel policy has made conservation payments the less profitable option on much of the same acreage, so solar income can be the thing that makes a conservation practice affordable that was not affordable before [@sturchio2025croplands]. That is the clearest published statement of the mechanism this lexicon calls [coexistence](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions): restoration paid for by the enterprise rather than by the field.

::: {.how-to}
**Name the recipients separately.** "The community" is not one party, and a benefit to one can be a loss to another, so this function is only legible once the actors are pulled apart:

- **Landowner** — lease and royalty income; the party a land payment reaches first, and often the only one it reaches.
- **Tenant farmer** — frequently the party who *loses*. Nearly 40% of agricultural land in California's Central Valley is rented or leased, and the leading analysis of agrisolar economics there assumes returns reach landowning or partial-owning farmers, naming that assumption as one of its own limitations [@stid2025]. A conversion that sustains an owner can end the operation of the person actually farming the ground. This is the sharpest misalignment in the set, and the one a lease-income argument most often hides.
- **Farm operation and succession** — whether the enterprise itself survives, which is the test [S3 coexistence](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) applies.
- **Neighboring residents** — bear viewshed, construction traffic, and glare, usually without a payment; the party [screening](7-terminology.qmd#term-screening) and good-neighbor agreements address.
- **Local government** — PILOT and tax base, against service and road costs.
- **Tribal nations and communities of place** — treaty rights, cultural landscapes, and consultation standing that do not reduce to a payment.
- **Workers** — construction and O&M wages, and whether they are local and durable rather than transient.
- **Subscribers and ratepayers** — community-solar savings, which may accrue well outside the host community entirely.

A project can score well on one of these and badly on the rest. Naming them separately is what keeps "community benefit" from collapsing into "somebody was paid."
:::

**Design dependencies.** The institutional levers are primary: ownership and control structure, offtake structure, and the [community-benefit](7-terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) instruments (CBA / HCA, PILOT, good-neighbor payments, community-solar subscription, local hiring, co-ownership). [Screening](7-terminology.qmd#term-screening) and edge treatment carry the livability sub-capacity on the visual side. Unlike the biophysical functions this one is not much bounded by scale zone or sharing position, since it is reachable across the transect, but its *character* shifts with scale: a farmstead array serves one household's resilience, a utility array a jurisdiction's tax base.

**Which sites can deliver it.** Reachable at every position, because every project has a host, but its dominant currency changes along the transect. At the farmstead and small-parcel end it is private economic resilience; at utility scale it is fiscal base, local hiring, and subscriber access. It is most at risk where a project is developer-owned, absentee, and offers benefit without engagement; most fully realized under locally-owned or co-ownership models with early, genuine participation.

**Point of use.** Not a distance. This function travels along tenure, contract, and jurisdiction rather than outward from the array, so the ranges that order the other four do not apply to it. A lease reaches whoever holds title, who may live in another state; PILOT revenue stops at a taxing boundary drawn for reasons having nothing to do with how far the effects carry; community-solar savings can reach subscribers in a different county; wages go wherever the crews come from. The question is therefore along which channel, and to whom, which is why the recipients above are named one at a time instead of drawn as a radius. The neighbor half a mile down the road, holding a viewshed and no payment, sits well inside every biophysical range and outside every economic one.

::: {.evidence}
**Evidence status.** The design principle is **verified** in the ecovoltaic frameworks themselves, where @tolgyesi2023 make a viable business model with embedded stakeholder engagement one of five co-equal pillars. The burden side is better measured than the benefit side: who gains and who bears the costs [@bessette2024], and property-value effects across six US states [@elmallah2023]. The benefit mechanisms are real and documented but sit largely in **gray literature** rather than peer-reviewed synthesis. The function is widely practiced and its instruments well known; which structures deliver durable, fairly-shared benefit is still thinly evidenced.
:::

## 4.6 Where each function applies {#sec-benefit-range}

A function is produced in one place and used in another, and the two are frequently not the same ground. Ecosystem-service research treats this as its central spatial problem, since the area that *provides* a service and the area that *benefits* from it differ often enough that they have to be mapped separately [@syrbe2012]. The distinction earns its place here for a plain reason. A restorative claim cannot be checked until it says where the benefit goes and who receives it, because "this project delivers a hydrologic function" might mean moisture held under the panels or nitrogen kept out of a creek three miles downstream, and those two need different evidence, reach different people, and answer different objections.

The lexicon calls this a function's **benefit delivery**. It is a different question from the [restoration mode](7-terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode) (§1.3), which asks how the restorative work gets done rather than where its result goes, and from the [influence zone](7-terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence), which is how far the array physically reaches. Influence and benefit come apart in both directions: relieving an aquifer is felt well outside any influence zone, and an array's influence extends over ground that gains nothing from it.

![How each function is delivered. Proximity and preservation both have a geography, but only proximity can be observed: preservation is ground nearby that stayed as it was, so it is drawn as a parcel that was never built. Channel has no geography, moving instead along tenure, contract, and jurisdiction.](../figures/fig_benefit_range.svg){#fig-benefit-range}

Benefits reach people in three ways. Two of them have a geography, though only one can be observed directly, and the third has no geography at all.

**Delivered by proximity.** The biophysical functions are delivered across ground, in four bands. Costanza's terms are given in italics, because they are what the literature uses.

- **On-site** (*in situ*) — point of production and point of use are the same ground: soil carbon, soil moisture, and the microclimate under the panels. The easiest band to measure and the easiest to over-claim from, since it says nothing at all about anywhere else.
- **Adjacent** (*local proximal*) — the near surroundings, at roughly the distance a pollinator forages or a viewshed carries. This is the best-quantified spillover in agrisolar (§4.3), and it runs both ways, carrying habitat and pollination outward while bringing [screening](7-terminology.qmd#term-screening) and glare in as obligations. **Solar fallowing** sits here too, meaning irrigated cropland retired beside an array rather than under it, 968 ha across 58 Central Valley installations, apparently funded by array revenue [@stid2025].
- **Downstream** (*directional flow related*) — carried by flow, so the benefit is used wherever the water goes: infiltration, runoff, sediment, nutrient export [@yavari2022; @schulte2017]. Direction defines this band rather than distance, since ground upslope of a problem can fix it and identical ground downslope cannot.
- **Regional and global** (*global non-proximal*) — the basin, the aquifer, the habitat network, and at the limit the atmosphere. Retiring irrigated ground eases an overdraft across a whole management area [@stid2022; @stid2025], and grassland habitat reads at the scale of a bird population rather than a parcel [@walston2025]. Carbon sits at the far end, benefiting everywhere and no one in particular, which is why it needs a market or a policy behind it before it is worth anything to the person holding the land.

One case in this family runs the other way. Demonstration sites, extension field days, farm tours, and school visits deliver their value by bringing people to the array rather than by sending anything out from it, which is a substantial part of what [Jack's Solar Garden](5-archetypes.qmd#arch-vegetable) (§5) produces. Costanza has a category for it, *user movement related*, and it is among the easiest things to design for and the most often left to chance.

**Delivered by channel.** The [community and economic function](#sec-fn-community) (§4.5) does not travel outward from the array at all. It moves along tenure, contract, and jurisdiction, which is a route rather than a radius. A lease reaches whoever holds title, who may live in another state. PILOT revenue stops at a taxing boundary drawn for reasons that have nothing to do with how far the effects carry. Community-solar savings can reach subscribers in a different county, and wages go wherever the crews come from. Asking how far this function carries is the wrong question, and asking along which channel and to whom is the right one, which is why §4.5 names its recipients one at a time instead of drawing a radius around the site.

**Delivered by preservation.** [Land sparing](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) delivers nothing that moves. Its benefit is ground somewhere else that stayed as it was, which makes this the one mode that is counterfactual rather than observed. It is still proximate, and that is easy to miss. Development pressure is local, since a developer assembling acreage near a substation chooses among parcels within a fairly narrow radius, so the ground a project spares is realistically ground in the same county rather than land in another state. That is what gives the claim somewhere to be checked: a preservation claim is tested against the local land market and the sites that were genuinely in play, not against an unbounded alternative. Ecosystem-service classification has no room for the mode at all, since it assumes a service that exists somewhere, so it is the lexicon's own addition rather than borrowed theory. The benefit is real and unusually hard to verify, which is why sparing claims earn the scrutiny [§2.2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-wedge) gives them.

::: {.how-to}
**What naming the delivery settles.** Three questions that are otherwise easy to run together.

1. **Who can verify it.** On-site claims can be measured on the site. Downstream and regional claims need a gauge, a well, or a model somewhere else, and preservation claims need the local land market and a credible account of what would otherwise have been built there. The further a benefit travels from the parcel, the more the burden of proof travels with it.
2. **Who captures it.** A landowner captures on-site benefit and can be paid for it. Downstream and regional benefits accrue to people holding no contract with the project, which is why they generally need a policy, a market, or a watershed authority behind them before they amount to more than goodwill.
3. **Which objection it answers.** This also explains why some arguments about a project never meet. A neighbor objecting to the view is describing something delivered at the fence line, and a developer answering with a carbon figure is describing something delivered everywhere and to no one in particular. Both statements can be true at the same time, and neither is a reply to the other. Naming how each benefit is delivered is what makes that mismatch visible instead of leaving it as mutual frustration.
:::

## 4.7 The SCALE footprint {#sec-scale}

SCALE reads a project across **Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy**, each from regeneration to depletion. Communities aligns with the community and economic function; Landscapes with the biophysical functions; Agriculture with continuity and the sharing–sparing axis; Energy with the design pressures. The reading is evaluative, but it has no pass mark or threshold (§8, issue 5).

![The SCALE footprint: a project's influence read across four domains (Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, Energy) and their sub-axes, each running from regeneration at the center to depletion at the rim. The reading is evaluative by design, which is what *restorative* commits the document to, but it is a direction of travel rather than a pass mark; no threshold line is drawn (§8, issue 5). The polygon shown is a worked example.](../figures/fig_scale_footprint.svg){#fig-scale}
